subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Electric Cars Came First
description: A 60-second lesson on Electric Cars Came First.

hook.text: Most people think electric cars are new. They actually outsold gasoline cars in 1900.

buildup.text: Early electrics were quiet, clean, and easy to start—no hand-cranking like gas cars.

discovery.text: In 1899, an electric car called La Jamais Contente was the first vehicle to break 60 mph.

twist.text: But batteries were heavy and range was short. When cheap gasoline arrived, electrics faded fast.

climax.text: By 1920, gas cars dominated completely. Electric vehicles vanished for almost a century.

punchline.text: The EV revolution is actually a comeback story.

quiz.question: What happened to electric cars by 1920?

details.summary: Electric vehicles outsold gasoline cars in the early 1900s, prized for their quiet operation and easy starting, before cheap gasoline and Ford's Model T shifted the market to combustion engines.
details.whyItMatters: Knowing that EVs are not a new invention but a revival reframes the current transition. The same advantages that attracted early adopters are winning buyers again today.
takeaways: Electric cars held a third of the US market around 1900
They were preferred for short urban trips by wealthy buyers
The electric starter and cheap gasoline killed early EV momentum

faq.question: Why did electric cars lose to gasoline cars the first time?
faq.answer: Gasoline offered far greater range, fuel was cheap and widely available, and Ford's assembly line made gas cars affordable. The invention of the electric starter eliminated the difficult hand crank.

faq.question: Were there charging stations for early electric cars?
faq.answer: Yes. Cities had battery charging and swapping stations in the early 1900s. Thomas Edison's company sold home charging systems, creating an early version of today's EV infrastructure.
